This book walks through a complete analysis of complex survey data in R, from downloading
the raw file to reporting a multivariable model:

1. importing a large survey file (@sec-import);
2. cleaning and recoding it with explicit checks (@sec-cleaning);
3. describing the population with survey-weighted statistics (@sec-descriptives);
4. multiple imputation of missing data that respects the survey design (@sec-imputation);
5. bivariate (crude) models (@sec-bivariate);
6. multivariable (adjusted) models, a sensitivity analysis, and reporting
   (@sec-multivariable).

It is written for students who know some R and the basics of regression, and who are new to
survey weights or multiple imputation.

## The question

**Is household income associated with diabetes among US adults?** Diabetes is common, costly,
and unequally distributed. Income shapes access to healthy food, safe places to be active,
health care, and the time and resources to manage a chronic condition. We estimate how the
prevalence of diabetes differs across income groups, before and after accounting for age,
sex, and race and ethnicity. An exercise in @sec-multivariable repeats the analysis for fair
or poor general health.

## The data

We use the 2024 [Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System](https://www.cdc.gov/brfss/)
(BRFSS): telephone interviews with 457,670 adults, weighted to represent the US adult
population. The data are public. You download them yourself (@sec-import) and they stay on
your computer.

## Setup

1. Install [R](https://cran.r-project.org/) (version 4.6.1 was used to build this book),
   [Quarto](https://quarto.org/docs/get-started/), and an editor such as
   [RStudio](https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/) or
   [Positron](https://positron.posit.co/).
2. Open the project: double-click `survey-weighted-analyses.Rproj` (RStudio) or open the
   folder (Positron).
3. Install the packages: in the R console, run `renv::restore()`. This installs the exact
   package versions the book was built with into the project (see @sec-reproducibility).
4. For interactive chunks, run `setwd("book")` in the R console first. Download
   the data by opening `book/01-import.qmd` and running the `download` chunk once.

Then render the book from the terminal with `quarto render book` (the result is
`book/_book/index.html`), or run the chapters' code chunk by chunk, in order. Each chapter saves
what the next one needs in `data/processed/`. Rendering time depends on available
memory, processor cores and the number of imputations.

The import, survey tables, imputations and model fits reuse cached calculations
on subsequent renders (see @sec-descriptive-cache and @sec-reproducibility).
For descriptive statistics alone, run Chapters 1–3 and stop there.

For a quick test of the whole pipeline, `quarto render book --profile smoke` uses 2 imputations
instead of `r n_imputations_book` and writes to separate folders (`book/_book-smoke/`,
`data/processed-smoke/`), so it never replaces the real results.

## Chapters

| Chapter | What it does | Saves |
|---|---|---|
| @sec-import | Downloads BRFSS 2024; reads the 13 variables we need | `01-brfss.rds` |
| @sec-cleaning | Declares and checks codebook values; recodes | `02-brfss-clean.rds`, `02-crosswalk.rds` |
| @sec-descriptives | Survey design; Tables 1 and 2; prevalence; design effects; missing data | |
| @sec-imputation | Multiple imputation (`r n_imputations` imputations) | `04-imputed.rds` |
| @sec-bivariate | Crude prevalence ratios, pooled with Rubin's rules | `05-crude.rds` |
| @sec-multivariable | Adjusted prevalence ratios; joint test; complete-case comparison; reporting | |
| @sec-decisions | Every coding decision, with counts | |
| @sec-reproducibility | Packages, seeds, smoke tests, session information | |

## How the code is written

- Every function is called with its package name, as in `dplyr::mutate()`, so you always
  know where a function comes from (and packages cannot silently mask each other).
- `|>` is R's pipe: `x |> f()` means `f(x)`.
- Lines that start with `# Check:` stop the code with an error if an assumption about the
  data fails. A silent check means the data are as expected.
- `tidylog::` versions of `dplyr` verbs print what each step did (rows dropped, variables
  created, share missing).
